characters.name: Foreman
characters.summary: The Foreman is Juror No. 1 and has the job of keeping the discussion and voting organised. He is not one of the strongest voices in the argument, but repeatedly tries to maintain order, count votes and keep the group moving through an increasingly heated and difficult deliberation.

characters.name: 2nd Juror
characters.summary: The 2nd Juror is quiet, hesitant and easily overshadowed at first. As the discussion develops he becomes more willing to question the evidence and speak for himself. His growing confidence reflects the wider shift in the room from simply accepting the prosecution case to examining it carefully.

characters.name: 3rd Juror
characters.summary: The 3rd Juror is the strongest and most emotional advocate for a guilty verdict. Aggressive, certain and intensely competitive, he repeatedly clashes with the 8th Juror. Gradually it becomes clear that his feelings about his estranged son are tangled up with the case, leaving him as the final juror holding out for guilty.

characters.name: 4th Juror
characters.summary: The 4th Juror is calm, controlled and analytical, and makes the strongest reasoned case for guilt. Unlike the 3rd or 10th Jurors, he is willing to change his mind when evidence is undermined. His final confidence rests on the woman eyewitness until the detail of her glasses creates reasonable doubt.

characters.name: 5th Juror
characters.summary: The 5th Juror grew up in a slum and reacts strongly when the others make assumptions about people from that background. Initially reserved, his own experience becomes crucial later when he explains how a switch-knife is actually used, seriously weakening the prosecution’s account of the stabbing.

characters.name: 6th Juror
characters.summary: The 6th Juror is straightforward, practical and generally less argumentative than the dominant personalities around the table. He listens to the developing doubts and changes his position as the evidence is tested. He also has a strong instinct for basic fairness and respect in the way the jurors treat one another.

characters.name: 7th Juror
characters.summary: The 7th Juror is impatient, sarcastic and preoccupied with getting away to his baseball game. He wants a quick result more than a careful discussion and provides much of the play’s humour. When he eventually changes his vote simply to speed things up, the 11th Juror challenges him to take his responsibility seriously.

characters.name: 8th Juror
characters.summary: The 8th Juror begins as the only person voting not guilty. He does not claim to know that the boy is innocent; instead, he insists that a life deserves proper discussion and repeatedly tests apparently certain evidence. Patient and persistent, he gradually turns the room by creating reasonable doubt rather than trying to prove an alternative story.

characters.name: 9th Juror
characters.summary: The 9th Juror is the oldest juror and the first to support the 8th, initially because he respects the courage of standing alone. He is observant and thoughtful about other people: his insight into the old witness helps undermine that testimony, and his observation of the 4th Juror’s spectacle marks leads to the decisive question about the woman’s eyesight.

characters.name: 10th Juror
characters.summary: The 10th Juror is loud, impatient and openly prejudiced against people from the boy’s background. His certainty about guilt is repeatedly driven by generalisations rather than the particular evidence. His long outburst late in Act Two isolates him from the rest of the jury as they physically and intellectually reject his prejudice.

characters.name: 11th Juror
characters.summary: The 11th Juror is thoughtful, courteous and unusually conscious of the responsibility involved in jury service. He asks careful questions rather than taking sides for their own sake. Later, when the 7th Juror changes his vote casually, the 11th challenges him sharply for treating a man’s life as something unimportant.

characters.name: 12th Juror
characters.summary: The 12th Juror works in advertising and often speaks in its language. He is sociable and talkative but less certain than the stronger personalities around him, changing his mind as different arguments seem persuasive. His uncertainty helps show how difficult it can be to distinguish confidence from genuinely convincing evidence.

characters.name: Judge
characters.summary: The Judge is heard only at the opening, setting out the jury’s responsibility and the standard of reasonable doubt. It is a brief but important framing role: his instructions establish that the verdict must be unanimous and that a guilty verdict will mean a mandatory death sentence.

characters.name: Guard
characters.summary: The Guard is a small practical role connecting the jury room to the world outside it. He brings the jurors into the room, checks on them after the argument at the end of Act One, and finally comes to collect them once they have reached their verdict.

beats.title: Into the jury room
beats.summary: The jurors arrive, settle in and reveal their personalities. Most expect the case to be disposed of quickly.

beats.title: Eleven to one
beats.summary: The first vote leaves the 8th Juror alone. He does not claim the boy is innocent; he insists that they should talk before sending him to die.

beats.title: Why he's guilty
beats.summary: The jurors begin going around the table, laying out the prosecution case: the witnesses, the boy's alibi, motive and record.

beats.title: The boy and his father
beats.summary: The discussion becomes more personal. The 3rd Juror reveals his broken relationship with his son, the 5th reacts to assumptions about slums, and the 8th begins questioning the defence and witnesses.

beats.title: The identical knife
beats.summary: The murder weapon becomes the focus. The 8th Juror produces an identical knife, showing that the supposedly unique weapon may not be unique.

beats.title: The secret ballot
beats.summary: The 8th Juror calls a secret ballot and the 9th joins him. The room reacts to the 10–2 split, then the discussion resumes after a break.

beats.title: Could the old man hear it?
beats.summary: The old man's evidence is tested against the noise of the passing el train. The jurors begin to doubt whether he could have heard and identified the boy's voice.

beats.title: "I'm going to kill you"
beats.summary: The jurors question whether the boy's shouted threat was meant literally. The 5th Juror changes his vote, making it nine to three.

beats.title: Why did he come back?
beats.summary: The defence lawyer and the boy's return home are reconsidered. The 11th Juror develops reasonable doubt and changes his vote, making it eight to four.

beats.title: The old man's walk
beats.summary: The jurors reconstruct the old man's journey to his door. It takes forty-two seconds rather than fifteen, and the argument culminates in the 3rd Juror shouting that he will kill the 8th.

beats.title: Six to six
beats.summary: After the confrontation, another open vote produces a six–six split. The approaching storm mirrors the increasingly divided room.

beats.title: The storm / Hung jury?
beats.summary: As the storm breaks, frustration grows. The jurors argue about giving up and declaring a hung jury rather than reaching a verdict.

beats.title: Can you remember the movies?
beats.summary: The 8th Juror tests the 4th Juror's memory of films he saw only days earlier, weakening the argument that the boy's failure to remember his movie alibi proves he was lying.

beats.title: Psychiatry and reasonable doubt
beats.summary: The psychiatrist's evidence is reconsidered. A capacity or tendency for violence is distinguished from proof that this boy committed this murder.

beats.title: How do you use a switch-knife?
beats.summary: The stabbing angle is reconstructed. The 5th Juror's experience with switch-knives challenges the prosecution's version; the 7th changes his vote and is forced to explain why.

beats.title: The 10th Juror's prejudice
beats.summary: The 10th Juror launches into a prejudiced tirade. The others reject both him and his reasoning, and the 8th Juror identifies prejudice as an obstacle to judging the facts.

beats.title: The woman's glasses
beats.summary: The woman's eyewitness evidence becomes the last major case for guilt. Marks on her nose reveal that she wore glasses, raising doubt that she could have identified the boy from bed without them. The vote moves to eleven to one.

beats.title: It's not your boy
beats.summary: The 3rd Juror stands alone and tries to revive the discarded evidence. His feelings about his own son finally surface; he changes to not guilty and the jury is ready.

script.speaker: Judge
script.text: . . . and that concludes the court’s explanation of the legal aspects of this case. And now, gentlemen of the jury, I come to my final instruction to you. Murder in the first degree — premeditated homicide — is the most serious charge tried in our criminal courts. You’ve listened to the testimony and you’ve had the law read to you and interpreted as it applies to this case. It now becomes your duty to try and separate the facts from the fancy. One man is dead. The life of another is at stake. I urge you to deliberate honestly and thoughtfully. If there is a reasonable doubt — then you must bring me a verdict of ‘not guilty’. If, however, there is no reasonable doubt, then you must, in good conscience, find the accused guilty. However you decide, your verdict must be unanimous. In the event you find the accused guilty, the bench will not entertain a recommendation for mercy. The death sentence is mandatory in this case. I don’t envy your job. You are faced with a grave responsibility. Thank you, gentlemen.

script.speaker: Guard
script.text: All right, let’s move along, gentlemen.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Great idea! Maybe we can get him elected senator.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Well, I figured we might want to vote by ballots.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Hey, what’s that for?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Sure they locked the door. What’d you think?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: I don’t know. It just never occurred to me.

script.speaker: Guard
script.text: Okay, gentlemen. There’s water. There’s an air-conditioner on the place. I almost dropped dead in court. You think they’d at least air-condition this place.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Y’know something?

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: What?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: This better be fast. I got tickets to that ball game tonight. Yanks — Cleveland. We got this new kid pitching. He’s a bull, this kid.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: All right, gentlemen. Let’s take seats.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: This better be fast. I got tickets to a ball game tonight. Yanks — Cleveland. We got this new kid pitching. He’s a bull, this kid.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: How’d you like it?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: I don’t know. It was pretty interesting.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I mean, I’ve never been on a jury before.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Well, I guess they’re entitled.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Sure they are. Everybody deserves a fair trial. That’s the system. Listen, I’m the last one to say anything against it, but I’m telling you sometimes I think we’d be better making these kids tougher. Y’know? Save us a lot of time and money.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Hey, how about getting started here?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Well, I was figuring we’d take a five-minute break. I mean, the old man’s in the bathroom . . .

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Are we going to sit in order?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: I don’t know.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Not a bad view.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: What d’you think of the case?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: I had a lot of interest for me. No dead spots — know what I mean? I’ll tell you, we were lucky to get a murder case. I heard us for a burglary or an assault or something. Those can be the—

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Funny.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: That’s right.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: . . . goddamn waste of time.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Yeah, can you imagine sitting there for three days just for this.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: And what about that business with the knife? I mean, asking grown-up people to believe that kind of bullshit—

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Well, look, you’ve gotta expect that. You know what you’re dealing with.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Yeah, I suppose so.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: And how. The kid’s no good. I mean, he’s got a record. He was in reform school and—

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Well, y’know, he was—

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: I mean, this is one of those cases. You know what I mean.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Yeah.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I didn’t get a chance to look at the newspapers today. Anything new going on?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I was just wondering how the market closed.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I wouldn’t know. Say, are you on the Exchange or something?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I’m a broker.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Really? I run a messenger service. The Beck and Call Company. The name is a kind of joke. I employ thirty-seven people . . . Started with nothing.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Hey, Mr Foreman, let’s go. What d’you say?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: All right, gentlemen. Let’s take seats.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: This better be fast. I got tickets to a ball game tonight. Yanks — Cleveland. We got this new kid pitching. He’s a bull, this kid.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: You’re a ball fan, aren’t you?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Where do you want us to sit?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Well, I was thinking we ought to sit in order, by jury numbers. Two, three, four, and so on. That’s the reason.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: What’s the difference?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I think it’s reasonable to sit according to number.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Let it be.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: What was your impression of the prosecuting attorney?

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: I beg pardon?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: I thought he was really sharp. I mean, the way he hammered home his points, one by one, in logical sequence. It takes a good brain to do that. I was very impressed.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: Yes, I think he did an expert job.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: I mean, he had a lot of drive, too. Real drive.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Okay, let’s get this show on the road.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: How about sitting down?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: How about sitting down?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Oh, I’m sorry.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: It’s pretty tough to figure, isn’t it? A kid kills his father. Bangs a knife that—

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Well, if you analyze the figures—

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: What figures? It’s those people! I’m telling you they let the kids run wild up here. Well, maybe it serves ’em right, know what I mean?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Hey, you a Yankee fan?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: No. Milwaukee.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Milwaukee! That’s like being hit on the head with a crowbar once a day.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: We’d like to get started.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: I’m sorry.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Milwaukee!

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: All right. Now you gentlemen can handle this any way you want to. I mean, I’m not going to have any rules. We can discuss it first and then vote, that’s one way. Or we can—

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Yeah, let’s vote. Who knows, maybe we can all go home.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: It’s up to you. Just let’s remember we’ve got a first degree murder charge here. If we vote ‘guilty’, we send the accused to the electric chair. That’s mandatory.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I think we all know that.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Come on, let’s vote.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Anybody doesn’t want to vote?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: That’s the law. Okay, are we ready? All those voting ‘guilty’ please raise your hands.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: . . . Nine — ten — eleven. That’s eleven for ‘guilty’. Okay. ‘Not guilty’?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Boy-oh-boy, there’s always one.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: So, what do we do now?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I don’t know.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Well, look, do you really think he’s innocent?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I don’t know.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I mean, let’s be reasonable. You sat in court and heard the same things we did. The man’s a dangerous killer. You could see it.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: The man? He’s sixteen years old.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Well, that’s old enough. He knifed his own father, four inches into the chest.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: It’s pretty obvious. I mean, I was convinced from the first day.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: I agree. Nobody proved otherwise. Would you like me to list them for you?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: No.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Then what do you want?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Nothing. I just want to talk.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: What’s there to talk about? Eleven men here agree. Nobody had to think twice about it, except you.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: I want to ask you something. Do you believe his story?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I don’t know whether I believe it or not. Maybe I don’t.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: So what’d you vote ‘not guilty’ for?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: There were eleven votes for ‘guilty’. It’s not easy for me to raise my hand and send a boy off to die without talking about it first.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Who says it’s easy for me?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: No one.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: What, just because I voted fast? I think the guy’s guilty. You couldn’t change my mind if you talked for a hundred years.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I’m not trying to change your mind. It’s just that we’re talking about somebody’s life here. I mean, we can’t decide in five minutes. Suppose we’re wrong?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Suppose we’re wrong? Suppose this whole building fell on my head. You can suppose anything.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: That’s right.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: What’s the difference how long it takes? We honestly think he’s guilty. So suppose we finish in five minutes? So what?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Let’s take an hour. The ball game doesn’t start till eight o’clock.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Okay, slugger, be my guest.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Well, who’s got something to say?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: I don’t mind telling you this, mister. We don’t owe him a thing. He got a fair trial, didn’t he? What d’you think that trial cost? He’s lucky he got it. Know what I mean? Look, we’re all grown-ups here. We heard the facts, didn’t we? Now, you’re not going to tell me that kid’s innocent. Look, you know how those people lie. I don’t have to tell you. They don’t know what the truth is. And lemme tell you, they don’t need any real big reason to kill someone, either. No sir. They get drunk. Oh, they’re very big drinkers, all of ’em. You know that. And bang, someone’s lying in the gutter. Nobody’s blaming them for it. That’s the way they are. By nature. You know what I mean? Violent!

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: I’m willing to put in an hour.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Well, now, who thinks he’s guilty? That’s what we’re sitting here for?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Maybe for no reason. I don’t know. Look, this boy’s been kicked around all his life. You know — living in a slum, his mother dead since he was nine. He spent a year and a half in an orphanage when his father was serving a jail term for forgery. That’s not a very happy beginning. He’s a wild, angry kid. That’s all he’s ever been. And you know why? Because he’s been hit on the head by somebody once a day, every day. He’s had a pretty miserable sixteen years. I think maybe we owe him a few words.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: I don’t mind telling you this, mister. We don’t owe him a thing. He got a fair trial, didn’t he? We heard the facts, didn’t we? Now, you’re not going to tell me that kid’s innocent.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: That’s not what I’m saying.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: What are we sitting here for?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: I’ve lived among ’em all my life. You can’t believe a word they say. You know that. I mean, they’re born liars.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: It suddenly occurs to me that you must be an ignorant man.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: What do you mean? What’s he talking about?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Do you think you have a monopoly on the truth?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: What are you making a Federal Case out of it for? How d’ya like this guy?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: I think certain things should be pointed out to this man.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: All right. It’s not Sunday. We don’t need a sermon in here.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Monopoly! For Chrissakes.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: If we’re going to discuss this case, let’s stick to the facts.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Right. We have a job to do. Let’s do it. Maybe if the gentleman who’s disagreeing down there could tell us why. You know, tell us what he thinks — we could show him where he’s probably mixed up.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Well, look, maybe this is an idea. I’m just thinking out loud, but it seems to me it’s up to us to convince this gentleman — that we’re right and he’s wrong. Maybe if we each took a minute or two. I mean, it’s just a quick thought . . .

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: No, I think it’s a good one. Supposing we go once around the table in order of jury numbers.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Anything. Let’s start it off.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Okay. That means you’re first.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Oh. Well — Well, it’s hard to put into words. I just — think he’s guilty. I thought it was obvious from the word go. I mean nobody proved otherwise.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Nobody has to prove otherwise. The burden of proof is on the prosecution. The defendant doesn’t have to open his mouth. That’s in the Constitution. You’ve heard of it.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Well, sure I’ve heard of it. I know what it is. I — what I meant — well, the man is guilty. I mean, somebody saw him do it.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Okay . . . Now, here’s what I think, and I have no personal feelings about this. I’m talking facts. Number one. Let’s take the old man who lived on the second floor right underneath the room where the murder took place. At ten minutes after twelve on the night of the killing he heard loud noises in the apartment upstairs. He said it sounded like a fight. Then he heard the kid shout out, ‘I’m gonna kill you.’ A second later he heard a body fall and he ran to the door of his apartment, looked out and saw the kid running down the stairs and out of the house. Then he called the police. They found the father with a knife in his chest.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: And the coroner fixed the time of the death at around midnight.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Right. I mean, there are facts for you. This boy is guilty. Look, I’m as sentimental as the

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: next guy. I know the kid is only sixteen, but he’s still got to pay for what he did.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: I’m with you, pops.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: It was obvious to me anyway, that the boy’s entire story was flimsy. He claimed he was at the movies during the time of the killing and yet one hour later he couldn’t remember what films he saw or who played in them.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: That’s right. Did you hear that? You’re absolutely right.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: No one saw him going into or out of the theatre.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Listen, what about that woman across the street? If her testimony don’t prove it, nothing does.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: That’s right. She was the one who actually saw the killing.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Let’s go in order here.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Just a minute. Here’s a woman . . . Here’s a woman who’s lying in bed and can’t sleep. She’s dying with the heat. Know what I mean? Anyway, she looks out the window and right across the street she sees the kid stick the knife into his father. The time is twelve ten on the nose. Everything fits. Look, she’s known the kid all his life. His window is right opposite hers, and she swore she saw him do it.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Through the windows of a passing elevated train.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Right. This el train had no passengers on it. It was just being moved downtown. The lights were out, remember? And they proved in court that at night you can look through the windows of an el train when the lights are out and see what’s happening on the other side. They proved it.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I’d like to ask you something.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Sure.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: You don’t believe the boy. How come you believe the woman? She’s one of ‘them’, too, isn’t she?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: You’re a pretty smart fellow, aren’t you?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Hey, let’s take it easy.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: What’s he so wise about? I’m telling you . . .

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Come on. Sit down. What are you letting him get you all upset for?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Let’s calm down now. Let’s try to keep it peaceful in here. Whose turn is it? Okay. How about you?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: I’ll pass it.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: That’s your privilege. How about the next gentleman?

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Well, I was looking for the motive. That’s very important. If there’s no motive, where’s the case? So anyway, that testimony from those people across the hall from the kid’s apartment, that was very powerful. Didn’t they say something about an argument between the father and the boy around seven o’clock that night? I mean, I can be wrong.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: It was eight o’clock. Not seven.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: That’s right. Eight o’clock. They heard an argument, but they couldn’t hear what it was about. Then they heard the father hit the boy twice, and finally they saw the boy walk angrily out of the house. What does that prove?

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Well, it doesn’t exactly prove anything. It’s just part of the picture.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: You said it revealed a motive for the killing. The prosecuting attorney said the same thing. Well, I don’t think it’s a very strong motive. This boy has been hit so many times in his life that violence is practically a normal state of affairs for him. I

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: can’t see two slaps in the face provoking him into committing murder.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: It may have been two slaps too many. Everyone has a breaking point.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Anything else?

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: No.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Okay. How about the next gentleman?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Me? I don’t know, it’s practically all said already. Look at his record. He was in Children’s Court when he was ten for throwing a rock at his teacher. At fourteen he was in Reform School. He stole a car. He’s been arrested for mugging. He was picked up twice for trying to slash another teenager with a knife. He’s real quick with switch knives, they said. This is a very fine boy.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Ever since he was five years old his father beat him up regularly. He used his fists.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: So would I. A kid like that.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Wouldn’t you call those beatings a motive for him to kill his father?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I don’t know. It’s a motive for him to be an angry kid. I’ll say that.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: It’s the kids, the way they are nowadays. Angry! Hostile! Just the way they talk to you. Listen, when I was his age I used to call my father ‘Sir’. You ever hear a boy call his father that any more?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Fathers don’t seem to think it’s important any more.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: No? Have you got any kids?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Two.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Yeah, well I’ve got one. He’s twenty. We did everything for that boy and what happened? When he was nine he ran away from a fight. I saw him. I was so ashamed I almost

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: threw up. So I told him right out, ‘I’m gonna make a man outa you or I’m gonna bust you in half trying.’ Well, I made a man outa him all right. When he was sixteen we had a battle. He hit me in the face. He’s big, y’know. I haven’t seen him in two years. Rotten kid. You work your heart out . . . All right. Let’s get on with it.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I think we’re missing the point here. We’re here to decide whether he’s guilty or innocent of murder, not to go into reasons why he grew up this way. Children from slum backgrounds are potential menaces to society. Now I think . . .

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: I’ve lived in a slum all my life. I nurse that trash in Harlem Hospital six nights a week.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Oh, now wait a second . . .

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: I used to play in a backyard that was filled with garbage. Maybe it still smells on me.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Now listen, buddy.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Now, let’s be reasonable. There’s nothing personal . . .

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: There is something personal!

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Come on, now. He didn’t mean you, feller. Let’s not be so sensitive.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: This sensitivity I understand.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: All right, let’s stop all this arguing. We’re wasting time here. It’s your turn. Let’s go.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I thought you were all supposed to be convincing me. Wasn’t that the idea?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Check. I forgot about that.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Well, what’s the difference? He’s the one who’s keeping us here. Let’s hear what he’s got to say.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Now just a second. We decided to do it a certain way. Let’s stick to what we said.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Ah, stop bein’ a kid, will you?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: A kid! Listen, what d’you mean by that?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: What d’ya think I mean? K-I-D, kid!

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: What, just because I’m trying to keep this thing organized? Listen. You want to do it? Here. You sit here. You take the responsibility. I’ll just shut up, that’s all.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Listen, what are you gettin’ so hot about? Calm down, will ya?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Don’t tell me to calm down. Here! Here’s the chair. You keep it goin’ smooth and everything. What d’ya think, it’s a snap? Come on, Mr Foreman. Let’s see how great you’d run the show.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Take it easy. The whole thing’s unimportant.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Unimportant? You want to try it?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: No. Listen, you’re doing a beautiful job. Nobody wants to change.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Yeah, you’re doing great. Hang in there and pitch.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: All right. Let’s hear from somebody.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Well, if you want me to tell you how I feel about it right now, it’s all right with me.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: I don’t care what you do.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: All right. I haven’t got anything brilliant. I only know as much as you do. According to the testimony the boy looks guilty. Maybe he is. I sat there in court for three days listening while the evidence built up. Everybody sounded so positive that I started to get a peculiar feeling about this trial. I mean, nothing is that positive. I had questions I would have liked to ask. Maybe they wouldn’t have meant anything. I don’t know. But I started to feel that the defence counsel wasn’t doing his job. He let too many things go. Little things.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: What little things? Listen, when these guys don’t ask questions, that’s because they know the answers already and they figure they’ll be hurt.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Maybe. It’s also possible for a lawyer to be just plain stupid, isn’t it?

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: You sound like you’ve met my brother-in-law.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I kept putting myself in the boy’s place. I would have asked for another lawyer, I think. Look, there was one alleged eyewitness to this killing. Someone else claims he heard the killing and then saw the boy running out afterwards. There was a lot of circumstantial evidence, but actually those two witnesses were the entire case for the prosecution. Supposing they were wrong?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: What do you mean, ‘Supposing they were wrong?’ What’s the point of having witnesses at all?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: They’re only people. People make mistakes. Could they be wrong?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: I . . . No! I don’t think so.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Do you know so?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Well, now, listen. Nobody can know a thing like that. This isn’t an exact science.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: That’s right. It isn’t.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: All right. Let’s try to get to the point here. What about the switch-knife they found in the father’s chest?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Well, wait a minute. I think we oughta . . . There are some people who haven’t talked yet. Shouldn’t we . . . ?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Look, they can talk whenever they like. Now just be quiet a second, will you? Okay, what about the knife? You know, the one that fine, upright boy admitted buying on the night of the murder. Let’s talk about that.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: All right, let’s talk about it. Let’s get it in here and look at it. I’d like to see it again. Mr Foreman?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: We all know what it looks like.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What are we gonna get out of seeing it again?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: You brought it up.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: The gentleman has a right to see exhibits in evidence. The knife, and the way it was bought, is pretty strong evidence. Don’t you think so?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I do.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Good. Now suppose we take these facts one at a time. One. The boy admitted going out of his house at eight o’clock on the night of the murder after being punched several times by his father.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: He didn’t say ‘punched’. He said ‘hit’.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: After being hit several times by his father. Two. The boy went directly to a neighbourhood junk shop where he bought a . . . What do you call these things—

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Switch-knives.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Switch-knives.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: — a switch-blade knife. Thank you.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Three. This wasn’t what you’d call an ordinary knife. It had a very unusual carved handle. Four. The storekeeper who sold it to him identified the knife in court and said it was the only one of its kind he had ever had in stock. Five. At, oh, about eight forty-five the boy ran into three friends of his in front of a diner. Am I correct so far?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Yes, you are.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: You bet he is. Now, listen to this man. He knows what he’s talking about.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: The boy talked with his friends for about an hour, leaving them at nine forty-five. During this time they saw the switch-knife. Six. Each of them identified the weapon in court as that same knife. Seven. The boy arrived home at about ten o’clock. Now this is where the stories offered by the boy and the State begin to diverge slightly. He claims that he stayed home until eleven thirty and then went to one of those all-night movies. He returned home at about three fifteen in the morning to find his father dead and himself arrested. Now, what happened to the switch-knife? He claims that the knife fell through a hole in his pocket some time between eleven thirty and three fifteen while he was on his trip to the movies and that he never saw it again. I think it’s quite clear that the boy never went to the movies that night. No one in the house saw him go out at eleven thirty. No one at the theatre identified him. He couldn’t even remember the names of the pictures he saw. What actually happened is this: the boy stayed home, had another fight with his father, stabbed him to death with the knife at ten minutes after twelve and fled from the house. He even remembered to wipe the knife clean of fingerprints. Everyone connected with the case identified the knife. Now are you trying to tell me that it really fell through a hole in the boy’s pocket and that someone picked it up off the street, went to the boy’s house and stabbed his father with it just to be amusing?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: No. I’m saying it’s possible that the boy lost the knife and that someone else stabbed his father with a similar knife. It’s possible.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Take a look at that knife. I’ve never seen one like it. Neither had the storekeeper who sold it to the boy. Aren’t you asking us to accept a pretty incredible coincidence?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I’m not asking anyone to accept it. I’m just saying that it’s possible.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: And I’m saying it’s not possible.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Look at it! It’s the same knife.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: What is this?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Where’d that come from?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What are you trying to do?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Quiet! Let’s be quiet. Where d’you get that knife?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I was walking for a couple of hours last night, just thinking. I walked through the boy’s neighbourhood. The knife comes from a little pawnshop three blocks from his house. It cost six dollars.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: It’s against the law to buy or sell switch-blade knives.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: That’s right. I broke the law.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Maybe there are ten knives like that. So what?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Maybe there are.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: So what does that mean? It’s the same kind of knife. So what’s that? The discovery of the age or something?

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: It would still be an incredible coincidence for another person to have stabbed the father with the same kind of knife.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: That’s right! He’s right.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: The odds are a million to one.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: It’s possible.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: But not very probable.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Listen, let’s take seats. There’s no point in milling around here.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: It’s interesting that he’d find a knife exactly like the one the boy bought.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What’s interesting? You think it proves anything?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Well, no. I was just . . .

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Interesting! Listen, how come the kid bought the knife to begin with?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Well, he claims that . . .

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I know. He claims he bought it as a present for a friend of his. He was gonna give it to him the next day because he busted the other kid’s knife dropping it on the pavement.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: That’s what he said.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Balcony!

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: The friend testified that the boy did break his knife.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Yeah. And how long before the killing? Three weeks. Right? So how come our noble lad bought this knife three and a half hours before they found it shoved up to here in the father’s chest?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Well, he was gonna give the knife to his friend. He just wanted to use it for a minute.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: If the boy bought the knife to use on his father, how come he showed what was going to be the murder weapon to three friends of his just a couple of hours before the killing?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Listen, all of this is just talk. The boy lied and you know it.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: He may have lied. Do you think he lied?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Now that’s a stupid question. Sure he lied.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Do you?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: You know my answer. He lied.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Do you think he lied?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: I’m not sure . . .

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: You’re not sure about what? Now wait a second. What are you, the kid’s lawyer or something? Who do you think you are to start cross-examining us?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Isn’t that what’s supposed to happen in a jury room?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Listen, there are still eleven of us in here who think he’s guilty.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Yeah. What do you think you’re gonna accomplish? You’re not gonna change anybody’s mind. So if you want to be stubborn and hang this jury, go ahead. The kid’ll be tried again and found guilty sure as he’s born.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: You’re probably right.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: So what are you gonna do about it? We can be here all night.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: It’s only one night. A boy may die.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Anybody got a deck of cards?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: I don’t think he ought to make a joke about it.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: What do you want me to do?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Listen, I don’t see what all this stuff about the knife has to do with anything. Somebody saw the kid stab his father. What more do we need? Let’s get done and get outa here.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Okay. These side arguments only slow us up. What about it?

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: You’re the only one.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I have a proposition to make to all of you. I want to call for a vote. I’d like you eleven men to vote by secret written ballot. I’ll abstain. If there are still eleven votes for guilty, we’ll take a guilty verdict in to the judge right now. But if anyone votes not guilty, we’ll stay and talk this thing out.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Well, finally you’re behaving like a reasonable man.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Check. I’ll buy that.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Okay. Let’s do it.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: That sounds fair.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Okay. Pass these along. Guilty. Guilty. Guilty. Guilty. Guilty. Guilty. Guilty. Guilty. Guilty. Not Guilty. Guilty.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: All right, who was it? Come on. I want to know.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: Excuse me. This was a secret ballot. We agreed on this.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Secret? What d’ya mean, secret? There are no secrets in a jury-room. I know who it was. Brother, you’re really something! You come in here and you vote guilty like everybody else, and then this golden-voiced preacher over here starts to tear your heart out with stories about a poor little kid who just couldn’t help becoming a murderer. So you change your vote. If that isn’t the most sickening . . .

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Now wait a minute. You can’t talk to me like that!

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: All right, let’s calm down.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Who does he think he is? I mean, did you see him?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Just sit down. He’s very excitable. Forget it. It doesn’t matter.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: You bet I’m excitable. We’re trying to put a guilty man into the chair where he belongs and all of a sudden somebody’s telling us fairy tales — and we’re listening.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Take it easy.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What do you mean — take it easy! D’you feel like seeing a proven murderer walking the streets? Why don’t we give him his knife back? Make it easier for him.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Okay, let’s stop the yelling. Who’s got something constructive to say?

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: Please. I would like to say something here. I have always thought that in this country a man was entitled to have unpopular opinions . . .

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Let’s stick to the subject. What made you change your vote?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: He didn’t change his vote. I did. Would you like me to tell you why?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: No, I wouldn’t like you to tell me why.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Well, I’d like to make it clear, anyway, if you don’t mind.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Do we have to listen to this?

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Hey, look! The man wants to talk.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Thank you. This gentleman— has been standing alone against us. He doesn’t say the boy is not guilty. He just isn’t sure. Well, it’s not easy to stand alone against the ridicule of others. He gambled for support and I gave it to him. I respect his motives. The boy on trial is probably guilty. But I want to hear more. For the time being the vote is ten to two.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: I think we ought to take a break. One man’s inside there. Let’s wait for him.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: goes into the wash-room and hangs his jacket on a hook.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Look, I was a little excited. Well, you know how it is — I didn’t mean to get nasty or anything.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Say, are you a salesman?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I’m an architect.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: You know what the soft sell is? You’re pretty good at it. What are ya getting out of it — kicks? The boy is guilty, pal. So let’s go home before we get sore throats.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: What’s the difference whether you get one here or at the ball game?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: No difference pal. No difference at all.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Nice bunch of guys.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I guess they’re the same as any.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: What a murderous day. You think we’ll be here much longer?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I don’t know.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: He’s guilty for sure. There’s not a doubt in the whole world. We should have been done already. You think he’s innocent?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I don’t know. It’s possible.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: I don’t know you, but I’m bettin’ you’ve never been wronger in your life. Y’oughta wrap it up. You’re wastin’ your time.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Suppose you were the one on trial?

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: I’m not used to supposing. But I’ll try one. Suppose you talk us all outa this and the kid really did knife his father?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Okay, let’s take seats.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Looks like we’ll be here for dinner.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Okay. Let’s get down to business. Who wants to start it off?

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Well, I’d like to make a point.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Maybe it would be profitable if we . . .

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: I didn’t mean to interrupt.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: No. Go ahead. It’s all right.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Well. I was going to say, well, this is probably a small point, but anyway . . . The boy had a motive for the killing. So if he didn’t do it, who did? Who else had the motive?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: As far as I know, we’re supposed to decide whether or not the boy on trial is guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. We’re not concerned with anyone else’s motives here. That’s a job for the police.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Very true. But we can’t help letting the only motive we know of creep into our thoughts, can we? And we can’t help asking ourselves who else might have had a motive. Logically, these things follow. This gentleman is asking a reasonable question. Somebody killed him. If it wasn’t the boy, who was it?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Modjelewski.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: You’re talking about the man I love!

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: If you haven’t got anything to add besides jokes, I suggest you listen.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Okay. It’s just letting off steam. I’m sorry. Go ahead.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Well, maybe you can answer me. Who else might have killed the father?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Well, I don’t know. The father wasn’t exactly a model citizen. He was in prison once. He was known to be a compulsive gambler and a pretty consistent loser. He spent a lot of time in neighbourhood bars and he’d get into fist fights sometimes after a couple of drinks. Usually over a woman. So here are a few possibilities. He could have been murdered by one of many men he served time with in prison. By a bookmaker. By a man he’d beaten up. By a woman he’d picked up. By any one of the people he was known to hang out with.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Boy-oh-boy, that’s the biggest load of crap I ever . . . Listen, we know the father was a bum. So what has that got to do with anything?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I didn’t bring it up. I was asked who else might have killed him. I gave my answer.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: That gentleman over there asked a direct question.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Everyone’s a lawyer!

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Look, the old man who lived downstairs heard the kid yell out, ‘I’m going to kill you.’ A split second later he heard a body hit the floor. Then he saw the kid run out of the house. Now what does all that mean to you?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: I don’t know. About ten or twelve seconds, maybe.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: That sounds right to me.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: What would you say?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Ten seconds. Approximately.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: All right. Say ten seconds. What are you getting at?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: This. It takes a six-car el train ten seconds to pass a given point. Now say that given point is the open window of the room in which the killing took place. You can almost reach out the window of that room and touch the el tracks. Right?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Right.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: All right. Now let me ask you this – has anyone here ever lived right next to the el tracks?

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Well, I just finished painting an apartment that overlooked an el line. I’m a house painter, y’know. I was there for three days.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: What was it like?

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: What d’ya mean?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I lived in a second-floor apartment next to an el line once. When the window’s open and the train goes by, the noise is almost unbearable. You can’t hear yourself think.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Okay. You can’t hear yourself think. Will you get to the point?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I will. Let’s take two pieces of testimony and try to put them together. First, the old man in the apartment downstairs. He says he heard the boy say, ‘I’m going to kill you’ and a split second later he heard the body hit the floor. One second later. Right?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: That’s right.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Second, the woman in the apartment across the street. She claimed that she looked out of her window and saw the killing through the last two cars of a passing elevated train. Right? The last two cars.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: All right. What point are you making here?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Now, we agreed that an el train takes about ten seconds to pass a given point. Since the woman saw the stabbing through the last two cars we can assume that the body fell to the floor just as the train passed by. Therefore, the el train had been roaring by the old man’s window for a full ten seconds before the body fell. The old man, according to his own testimony, hearing ‘I’m going to kill you’ and the body falling a split second later, would have had to hear the boy make this statement while the el was roaring past his nose. It’s not possible that he could have heard it.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: That’s idiotic! Sure he could have heard it.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Do you think so?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: The old man said the boy yelled it out. That’s enough for me.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: If he heard anything at all, he still couldn’t have identified the voice with the el roaring by.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: You’re talking about a matter of seconds here. Nobody can be that accurate.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Well, I think that testimony which could put a human being into the electric chair should be that accurate.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: I don’t think he could have heard it.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Yeah. Maybe he didn’t hear it. I mean, with the el noise . . .

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What are you people talking about?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Well, it stands to reason . . .

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: You’re crazy! Why should he lie? What’s he got to gain?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Attention, maybe.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: You keep coming up with these bright sayings. Why don’t you send one in to a newspaper? They pay three dollars.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Hey! What’re ya talking to him like that for?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Get your hands off me!

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: It’s just that I looked at him for a very long time. He was a very old man with a torn jacket and he walked very slowly to the stand. He was dragging his left leg and trying to hide it because he was ashamed. I think I know him better than anyone here. This is a quiet, frightened, insignificant old man who has been nothing all his life, who has never had recognition, his name in the newspapers. Nobody knows him, nobody quotes him, nobody seeks his advice after seventy-five years. That’s a very sad thing, to be nothing. A man like this needs to be recognized, to be listened to, to be quoted just once. This is very important. It would be so hard for him to recede into the background . . .

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Now, wait a minute. Are you trying to tell us he’d lie just so that he could be important once?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: No. He wouldn’t really lie. But perhaps he’d make himself believe that he’d heard those words and recognized the boy’s face.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Well, that’s the most fantastic story I’ve ever heard. How can you make up a thing like that? What do you know about it?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Gentlemen, this case is based on a reasonable and logical progression of facts. Let’s keep it there.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: Facts may be coloured by the personalities of the people who present them.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Anybody want a cough drop?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: I’ll take one. Thanks.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Say what you like, I still don’t see how anybody can think the boy’s not guilty.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I think we’ve proved that the old man couldn’t have heard the boy say, ‘I’m going to kill you’, but supposing . . .

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: You didn’t prove it at all. What are you talking about?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: But supposing he really did hear it. This phrase, how many times has each of us used it? Probably hundreds. ‘I could kill you for that, darling.’ ‘If you do that once more, Junior, I’m going to kill you.’ We say it every day. It doesn’t mean we’re going to kill someone.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Wait a minute! The phrase was, ‘I’m going to kill you,’ and the kid screamed it out at the top of his lungs. Don’t tell me he didn’t mean it. Anybody says a thing like that the way he said it, they mean it.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Well, gee, I don’t know. I remember I was arguing with the guy I work next to at the bank a couple of weeks ago; so he called me an idiot; so I yelled at him . . .

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: No listen, this guy is making you believe things that aren’t so. The kid said he was going to kill him and he did kill him.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Do you really think the boy would shout out a thing like that so the whole neighbourhood would hear it? I don’t think so. He’s much too bright for that.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Bright? He’s a common, ignorant slob. He don’t even speak good English.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: He doesn’t even speak good English.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: I’d like to change my vote to ‘not guilty’.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Now you’ve got to be kidding.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: You heard.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Are you sure?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Yes, I’m sure.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: The vote is nine to three in favour of ‘guilty’.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Well, if that isn’t the livin’ end! What are you basing it on? Stories this guy made up. Listen, there are facts staring you right in the face. Every one of them says this kid killed his old man. For cryin’ out loud, his own lawyer knew he didn’t stand a chance right from the beginning. You could see it. He deserves the chair.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Does he? It’s happened before that someone’s been convicted of murder and executed, and years later someone else has confessed to the crime. Sometimes . . . Sometimes the facts that are staring you in the face are wrong!

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: I’m talkin’ to him – not to you. Boy, this guy is really something. Listen, the kid had a lawyer, didn’t he? The lawyer presented his case, not you. How come you’ve got so much to say?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: The lawyer was court-appointed.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: So what does that mean?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: It could mean he didn’t want the case. It could mean he resented being appointed. It’s the kind of case that brings him nothing. He’d really have to believe in his client to make a good fight. As you pointed out a minute ago, he obviously didn’t.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Sure he didn’t. Who in hell could, except God come to earth or somebody? Come on already! Look at the time!

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: Pardon me, but I have made some notes here.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Notes yet!

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: I would like please to say something. I have been listening very closely, and it seems to me that this man – has some very good points to make. From what was presented at the trial the boy looks guilty, but maybe if we go deeper . . .

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Come on, willya?

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: There is a question I would like to ask. We assume that the boy committed murder. He stabbed his father in the chest and ran away. This was at ten minutes after twelve. Now, how was he caught by the police? He came home at three o’clock or so and was captured by two detectives in the hallway of his house. My question is, if he really had killed his father, why would he come back three hours later? Wouldn’t he be afraid of being caught?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Look – he came home to get his knife. It’s not nice to leave knives sticking around in people’s chests.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Yeah, especially relatives’.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: The boy knew that there were people who could identify the knife as the one he had just bought. He had to get it before the police did.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: But if he knew the knife could be identified, why did he leave it there in the first place?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Well, I think we can assume he ran out in a state of panic after he killed his father, and then when he finally calmed down, he realized that he had left the knife there.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: If I were the boy and I had killed my father, I would not have come home three hours later. I would be afraid that the police would be there. I would stay away, knife or no knife.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Listen, you voted ‘guilty’, didn’t you? What side are you on?

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: I don’t believe I have to be loyal to one side or the other. I am simply asking questions.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Well, this is just off the top of my head, but if I were the boy, and I’d, you know, done the stabbing and everything, I’d take a chance and go back for the knife. I’ll bet he figured no one had seen him and that the body probably wasn’t even discovered yet. After all, it was the middle of the night. He probably thought no one would find the body till the next day.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: Pardon. Here is my whole point. The woman across the street testified that a moment after she saw the killing, that is, a moment after the el train went by, she screamed and then went to telephone the police. Now, the boy must certainly have heard that scream and known that somebody saw something. I don’t think he would have gone back if he had been the murderer.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Two points. One: in his state of panic he may not have heard the scream. Perhaps it wasn’t very loud. Two: if he did hear it, he may not have connected it with his own act. Remember, he lived in a neighbourhood where screams were fairly commonplace.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Right! There’s your answer.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Maybe. Maybe he did stab his father, didn’t hear the woman’s scream, did run out in a panic, did calm down three hours later and come back to try to get the knife, risking being caught by the police. Maybe all those things are so. But maybe they’re not. I think there’s enough doubt to make us wonder whether he was there at all during the time the murder took place.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: What d’ya mean doubt? What are you talking about? Did or didn’t the old man see the kid running out of the house at twelve ten?

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: He says he did.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Says he did! Boy-oh-boy! How do you like that? You’re makin’ out like it don’t matter what people say. What d’ya think these people get up on the witness stand for – their health? I’m telling you men the facts are being changed around here. Witnesses are being doubted and there’s no reason for it.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Witnesses can make mistakes.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Sure, when you want ’em to, they do! Know what I mean?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Okay. Let’s hold the yelling down.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: You keep saying that. Maybe what we need is a little yelling in here. These guys are going off every which way. Did hear the scream, didn’t hear the scream. What’s the difference? They’re just little details. You’re forgetting the important stuff. I mean, all of a sudden here everybody . . .

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I’d like to call for another vote.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: There’s another vote called for. How about taking seats?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What are we gonna gain by voting again?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: I don’t know. The gentleman asked . . .

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I never saw so much time spent on nothing.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: It only takes a second.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Okay. I guess the fastest way is to find out who’s voting not guilty. All those in favour of not guilty raise their hands. Still the same. One, two, three ‘not guilty’s. Nine ‘guilty’s.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: So now where are we? I’m telling you, we can yakety-yak until next Tuesday here. Where’s it getting us?

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: Pardon. I vote not guilty.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Oh, brother!

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Oh, now listen! What are you talking about? I mean, we’re all going crazy in here or something! This kid is guilty. Why don’tcha pay attention to the facts. Listen, tell him, will ya? This is getting to be a goddamn joke!

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: The vote is eight to four, favour of guilty.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I mean, everybody’s heart is starting to bleed for this punk little kid like the President just declared it ‘Love Your Underprivileged Brother Week’, or something. Listen, I’d like you to tell me why you changed your vote. Come on, give me reasons.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: I don’t have to defend my decision to you. I have a reasonable doubt in my mind.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What reasonable doubt? That’s nothing but words. Here, look at this. The kid you just decided isn’t guilty was seen ramming this thing into his father. Well, look at it, Mr Reasonable Doubt.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: That’s not the knife. Don’t you remember?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Brilliant!

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: I’m tellin’ ya, this is the craziest. Look, what about the old man? Are we supposed to believe that he didn’t get up and run to his door and see the kid tearing down the stairs fifteen seconds after the killing? He’s only saying he did to be important. I mean, what’s the point of the whole . . . ?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Did the old man say he ran to the door?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Ran. Walked. What’s the difference? He got there.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: He said he ran to the door. At least, I think he did.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: I don’t remember what he said. But I don’t see how he could run.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: He said he went from his bedroom to the front door. That’s enough, isn’t it?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Wait a minute. Where was his bedroom, again?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Down the hall somewhere. I thought you remembered everything. Don’t you remember?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: No. Mr Foreman, I’d like to take a look at the diagram of the apartment.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Why don’t we have them run the trial over just so you can get everything straight?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Mr Foreman . . .

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: I heard you.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: All right, what’s this for? How come you’re the only one in the room who wants to see exhibits all the time?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: I want to see this one, too.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: And I want to stop wasting time.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: We’re not. I’d like to see if a very old man who drags one leg when he walks because he had a stroke last year can get from his bed to his front door in fifteen seconds.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: He said twenty seconds.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: He said fifteen.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: He said fifteen.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: How does he know how long fifteen seconds is? You can’t judge that kind of thing.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: He said fifteen seconds. He was very positive about it.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: He’s an old man. You saw him. Half the time he was confused. How could he be positive about anything?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: I don’t see what we’re going to prove here. The man said he saw the boy running out.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Well, let’s see if the details bear him out. As soon as the body fell to the floor, he said, he heard footsteps upstairs running towards the front door. He heard the upstairs door open and the footsteps start down the stairs. He got to his front door as soon as he could. He swore that it couldn’t have been more than fifteen seconds. Now, if the killer began running immediately . . .

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Well, maybe he didn’t.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: The old man said he did.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: You know, you ought to be down in Atlantic City at that hair-splitters’ convention.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Listen, baseball, why don’t you stop making smart remarks all the time?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: May I? This is the apartment in which the killing took place. The old man’s apartment is directly beneath it and exactly the same. Here are the el tracks. The bedroom. Another bedroom. Bathroom. Living-room. Kitchen. And this is the hall. Here’s the front door to the apartment. And here are the stairs. Now, the old man was in bed in this room. He says he got up, went out into the hall, down the hall to the front door, opened it and looked out just in time to see the boy racing down the stairs. Am I right so far?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: That’s the story, for the nineteenth time.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Fifteen seconds after he heard the body fall.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: Correct.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: His bed was at the window. It’s forty-three feet, six inches. Now, he had to get up out of bed, walk twelve feet, open the bedroom door, walk forty-three feet and open the front door – all in fifteen seconds. Do you think he could have done it?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Sure he coulda done it.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: He can only walk very slowly. They had to help him into the witness chair.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: This is the old man’s bed.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: What’s going on here?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I want to try this thing. Let’s see how long it took him.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What d’you mean you want to try it? Why didn’t the kid’s lawyer bring it up, if it’s so important?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Well, maybe he just didn’t think of it.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: All right, here’s the bed. I’m going to pace off twelve feet, the length of the bedroom.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: You’re crazy. You can’t re-create a thing like that.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: I’d like to see it.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: All right, this is the bedroom door. The hall is a little over forty-three feet long. I’ll pace over to that wall and back again.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: . . . twelve . . . According to you it’ll only take fifteen seconds. We can spare that. . . . thirty-nine, forty, forty-one, forty-two, forty-three. Okay, pass me another chair, please. This is the door to the outside hall and stairway. It was chain-locked according to the testimony. Who’s got a watch with a second hand?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: I have.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: When you want me to start, stamp your foot. That’ll be the body falling. Time me from there.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Anyone for charades?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I’ve never seen anything like this in my whole life!

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Okay. I’m ready.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Come on, let’s go here.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: I want to wait until the second hand reaches sixty.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Come on. Snap it up. He walked twice as fast as that.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: This is, I think, even more quickly than the old man walked in the courtroom.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: If you think I should go faster, I will.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Come on, willya! Let’s get this kid’s stuff over with.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Stop!

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Right.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: What’s the time?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Fifteen – twenty – thirty – thirty-five – forty – forty-two seconds exactly.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Forty-two seconds!

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I think this is what happened. The old man heard the fight between the boy and his father a few hours earlier. Then, while lying in bed, he heard a body hit the floor in the boy’s apartment, and he heard the woman scream from across the street. He got up, tried to get to the door, heard someone racing down the stairs, and assumed it was the boy.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: I think that’s possible.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Well, you’re not getting away with it enough. What’s the matter with you people? Every one of you knows this kid is guilty. He’s got to burn. We’re letting him slip through our fingers here.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Slip through our fingers? Are you his executioner?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I’m one of ’em.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Maybe you’d like to pull the switch.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: For this kid? You bet I’d like to pull the switch.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I’m sorry for you.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Don’t start with me now.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Ever since we walked into this room you’ve been behaving like a self-appointed public avenger.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I’m telling you now! Shut up!

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: You want to see this boy die because you personally want it, not because of the facts.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Shut up!

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: You’re a sadist!

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Shut up! Let go of me, God damn it! I’ll kill him! I’ll kill him!

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: You don’t really mean you’ll kill me, do you?

script.speaker: Guard
script.text: Is there anything wrong, gentlemen? I heard some noise.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: No. There’s nothing wrong. Just a little argument. Everything’s OK. We’re finished with this.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Well, what are you staring at?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: It’s getting late. What do they do, take us out to a restaurant for supper?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: How do I know?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: I wonder if they let us go home in case we can’t finish tonight.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: This is not why we are here, to fight. We have a responsibility. We have nothing to gain— —or lose by our verdict. We should not make it a personal thing.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Look how dark it’s getting. We’re gonna have a storm. Boy, it’s hot. Pardon me, don’t you sweat?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: No. I don’t.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Uh, listen, I was wondering if maybe we shouldn’t take another vote.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Great idea. Maybe we can follow this one up with dancing and refreshments.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Mr Foreman?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: It’s all right with me. Anyone doesn’t want to vote?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I think we ought to have an open ballot. Call out your votes, y’know. Let’s see who stands where.
