script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: That sounds fair. Anyone object? The last vote was eight to four in favour of guilty. All right. I’ll call off your jury numbers. Vote guilty. Number Two?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Not Guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Number Three?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Number Four?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Number Five?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Not Guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Number Six?

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Not Guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Number Seven?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Number Eight?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Not Guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Number Nine?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Not Guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Number Ten?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Number Eleven?

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: Not Guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Number Twelve?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Six to six.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: And we go into extra innings here.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Six to six! I’m telling you, some of you people in here are out of your minds. A kid like that.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: I don’t think the kind of boy he is has anything to do with it. The facts are supposed to determine the case.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Ah, don’t give me any of that. I’m sick and tired of facts. You can twist ’em any way you like. Know what I mean?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: That’s exactly the point this gentleman has been making. I mean, you keep shouting at the top of your lungs . . . I’d like to be a little younger. It’s very hot in here.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: Do you want some water?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: No, thanks.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: It’s going to rain.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Tell me, how come you switched?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Well, it just seemed to me . . .

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: I mean, you haven’t got a leg to stand on. You know that, don’t cha?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Well, I don’t feel that way. There’re a lot of details that never came out.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Details! You’re just letting yourself get bulldozed by a buncha what d’ya call ’em – intellectuals.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Now, listen, I don’t think you have any right to . . . Loudmouth!

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Wow! Look at that come down, willya? Think it’ll cool things off?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Yeah, I guess so.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Hey, let’s try to get this fan goin’ in here. What d’ya say? It musta been connected to the light switch.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Some rain, huh? Well, what d’ya think of this thing? It’s even-steven. Kind of surprising, isn’t it?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Yes.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Listen, that business before, you know, where that guy was baiting me. I mean, that doesn’t prove anything. Listen, I’m a very excitable person, y’know. Anybody in his right mind’d blow his stack, wouldn’t he? He was just trying to bait me.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: He did an excellent job. Excuse me.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Well – isn’t this the goddamnedest thing you ever saw? Six to six. It’s a joke.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What are we gonna do about it? Can’t we break it somehow?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Those six bastards in there aren’t going to change their minds.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Five of them already have changed their minds. There’s no reason why they can’t be persuaded to do it again.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: How?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Just by using logic.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Logic! Holy cow!

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: You want my opinion?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Go ahead.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: I think we should just quit.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What the hell are you talking about?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Look, they’re not gonna switch, so let’s go and tell the Judge – we’ll be here all night. For Chrissakes, let’s tell him we’re hung.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Well, that’s the most ridiculous thing I ever . . . You took an oath in the courtroom. You can’t just quit.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Why not?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: It’s dishonest. Why don’t you vote not guilty?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: I voted guilty because I think he’s guilty.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: But now you don’t care what happens?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: No. Why should I?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: All right, let’s stop this. We’re not going to get anywhere like this.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Well, what does he want? I gave my honest opinion.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I know.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: I suppose you don’t think much of it?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: No, I don’t.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Uh – we’d like to get going in here again, if you don’t mind.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: How about him? Is that something?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: A hung jury doesn’t mean a thing. They just have to start the trial with another jury. That’s not what we’re here for.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: What the hell’s the difference? A hung jury is what you’re gonna get.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Look, would you please . . .

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Listen, I’ll tell you what I think. We’re goin’ nowhere here. I’m ready to walk into court right now and declare a hung jury.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I don’t think the court will accept a hung jury. We haven’t been in here very long.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Well, let’s find out.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: I am not in favour of this.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Listen, this kid wouldn’t stand a chance with another jury and you know it. Come on, we’re hung. Nobody’s gonna change his opinion. Let’s take it inside.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: You still don’t think there’s any room for reasonable doubt?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: No, I don’t.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: Pardon. Maybe you don’t fully understand the term ‘reasonable doubt’.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: All right. Let’s stop arguing for two minutes in here. Can’t we stick to the subject?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I’d like to go over something, if you gentlemen don’t mind. An important point for the prosecution was the fact that the boy, after he claimed he was at the movies during the hours the killing took place, couldn’t name the pictures he saw. or the stars who appeared in them. This gentleman has repeated that point in here several times.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: That’s correct. It was the only alibi the boy offered and he himself couldn’t back it up with any details at all.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Putting yourself in the boy’s place, if you can, do you think you’d be able to remember details after an upsetting experience such as being struck in the face by your father?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I think so, if there were any special details to remember. He couldn’t remember the movies at the theatre he named because he wasn’t there that night.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: According to the police testimony in court he was questioned by the police in the kitchen of his apartment while the body of his father was lying on the floor in the bedroom. Do you think you could remember details under such circumstances?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I do.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Under great emotional stress?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Under great emotional stress.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: He remembered the movies in court. He named them correctly and he named the stars who played in them.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Yes, his lawyer took great pains to bring that out. He had three months from the night of the murder to the day of the trial in which to memorize them.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I’d like to ask you a personal question.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Go ahead.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Where were you last night?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I was home.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: What about the night before last?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Come on, what is this?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: It’s perfectly all right. I went from court to my office and stayed there till eight thirty. Then I went straight home to bed.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: And the night before that?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: That was – Tuesday? I played bridge.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: And Monday night.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: When you get him down to New Year’s Eve, nineteen fifty lemme know.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Monday. Monday night. Monday night my wife and I went to the movies.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: What did you see?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: What was the second feature?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: The . . . I’ll tell you in a minute. Mrs – uh – Mainbridge. No, Bainbridge.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Excuse me. I saw that. It’s called

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Yes. I think that’s right.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Who was in

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Barbara – Long, I think.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Who else?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Well, I’d never heard of them before. It was a very inexpensive second feature, with unknown . . .

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: And you weren’t under an emotional strain, were you?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: No, I wasn’t.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: I think the point is made.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: What? Just because he can’t remember the name of some two-bit movie star? I suppose that proves the kid was at the movies.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: No. But it indicates that no one can prove he wasn’t. He might have been at the movies and forgotten what he saw. It’s possible.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: You can talk till your tongue is draggin’ on the floor. The boy is guilty. Period. Know what I mean, my friend? Who’s got those cough drops?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: They’re all gone, my friend.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Y’know, there’s something we’re forgetting here that I was just thinking about. Well, that’s the whole business that dragged out forever, y’know with the psychiatrist.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Now don’t start with all that phoney psycho-what-ever-you-call-it stuff. What a racket that is! Filling people’s heads with all that junk. Listen, I’ve got three psychiatrists keeping their cars in one of my garages. The whole three of ’em are crazy.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Why don’t you let the man talk? You can take five minutes on the uselessness of psychiatry when he’s finished.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: What I was gonna say was, the psychiatrist definitely stated that the boy had strong homicidal tendencies. Am I right?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Check. I think he said something about paranoid tendencies if I’m not mistaken.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: In discussing a thing as the murder potential we should remember that many of us are capable of committing murder. But few of us do. These psychiatric tests can accomplish along these lines is this: they can tell us that some day a particular person may commit a murder. That’s all. They prove nothing.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Then how come they’re admitted in evidence?

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: They have many uses, of course. In this case they added to the general impression the prosecution was trying to create. Yet none of that. To say that a man is capable of murder does not mean that he has committed murder.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: But it can mean it. Listen, if they said the kid is capable of killing, he could’ve killed couldn’t he?

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: What time is it?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: It’s five of six. Man, look at that rain.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: There goes your ball game.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Say, could I see that knife for a second?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Well, we’re still tied up six to six. Who’s got a suggestion?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: I have. Let’s get some dinner.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Why don’t we wait till seven? Give it another hour.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Okay with me.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Um – there’s something I’d like to say. I mean, it’s been bothering me a little and as long as we’re stuck . . . Well, there was this whole business about the stab wound and how it was made, the downward angle of it, you know?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Don’t tell me we’re gonna start with that. They went over it and over it.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: I know they did, but I don’t go along with it. The boy is five feet, seven inches tall. His father was six two. That’s a difference of seven inches. It’s a very awkward thing to stab down into the chest of someone who’s more than a half a foot taller than you are.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Give me that. Look, you’re not gonna be satisfied till you see it again. I’m gonna give you a demonstration. Somebody get up. Okay. Now, watch this. I don’t want to have to do it again. I’m six or seven inches shorter than you. Right?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: That’s right. Maybe a little more.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Okay. Let it be more.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: All right. There’s your angle. Take a look at it. Down and in. That’s how I’d stab a taller man in the chest and that’s how it was done. Now go ahead and tell me I’m wrong.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Down and in. I guess there’s no argument.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Wait a minute. Give me that. I hate these things. I grew up with them.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Have you seen them used in fights?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Too many of them. Funny, I wasn’t thinking of it. I guess you try to forget those things. You don’t use this kind of knife that way. You have to hold it like this to release the blade. In order to stab downwards, you would have to change your grip.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: How do you use it?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Underhanded. Like that. Anyone who’s ever used a switch-knife’d never handle it any other way.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Are you sure?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: I’m sure. That’s why they’re made like this.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Everyone agreed that the boy is pretty handy with a knife, didn’t they?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: That’s right.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Do you think he would have made the kind of wound that killed his father?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Not with the experience he’d had with these things. No, I don’t think he would. He’d go for him underhanded . . .

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I don’t think you can determine what type of wound this boy might or might not have made simply because he knows how to handle a knife.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: That’s right. That’s absolutely right.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: What do you think?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Well – I don’t know . . .

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What d’ya mean – you don’t know?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: I don’t know.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: What about you?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Just a minute. According to the woman across the street . . .

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Listen, I’ll tell you something. I’m a little sick of this whole thing already. All this yakkin’s gettin’ us nowhere so I’m going to break it up here. I’m changing my vote to not guilty.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: You’re what?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: You heard me. I’ve had enough.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What d’you mean – you’ve had enough? That’s no answer.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Hey, listen, you! Just worry about yourself.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: He’s right. That is not an answer. What kind of a man are you? You have sat here and voted guilty with everyone else because there are some baseball tickets burning a hole

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: God damn you. I don’t have to . . .

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: You do have to. Say it. Why?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: I – don’t think he’s guilty.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Mr Foreman, I want another vote.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Okay, there’s another vote called for. I guess the quickest way is a show of hands. Anybody object? All those voting not guilty raise your hands. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight. Nine. All those voting guilty. Nine to three in favour of not guilty.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: I don’t understand you people. I mean, all these picky little points you keep bringing up. They don’t mean nothing. How can you believe his story? You’re an intelligent man. Well, you’re not gonna tell me you’re not. You know the facts of life. Well, for Chrissakes look at what we’re dealing with here. You know what they’re like! Well, for instance, they don’t need any big excuse to kill someone. Well, that’s true. Everybody knows it. And when they’re drunk, and all of a sudden – bang – somebody’s lying dead in the gutter. Okay, nobody’s blaming them for it. That’s how they are, by nature, y’know what I mean? Violent! Human life don’t mean as much to them as it does to us. Where are you going? While you’re in there, clean out your ears, maybe you’ll hear something. Look, you listen to me now. These people are boozing it up, and fighting all the time, and if somebody gets killed, so somebody gets killed. They don’t care. Family don’t mean anything to them. They breed like animals. Fathers, mothers, that don’t mean anything. Oh sure, there are some good things about ’em. Look, I’m the first one to say that. I’ve know some who were okay, but that’s the exception.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Do you know you’re a sick man?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Sick?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Why don’t you sit down?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: What the hell are you? No. Who the hell is he to tell me that? Sick. Look at him – he can hardly stand up. Listen, I’m speaking my piece here and you’re gonna listen.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Maybe if you just quieted down.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: I will like hell quiet down. Now let me lay this out for you ignorant bastards. You at the window, you’re so goddamned smart. We’re facing a danger here. Don’t you know it? These people are multiplying. That kid on trial, his type, they’re multiplying five times as fast as we are. That’s the statistic. Five times. And they are – wild animals. They’re against us, they hate us, they want to destroy us. That’s right. Don’t look at me like that! For God’s sake, we’re living in a dangerous time, and if we don’t watch it, then they are gonna own us. They’re gonna breed us out of existence.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Ah, shut up!

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: I’m warning you. This boy, this boy on trial here. We’ve got him. That’s one at least. I say get him before his kind gets us. I don’t give a goddamn about the law. Why should I? They don’t. Now I’m telling you.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: I’ve heard enough. Now you just stop all this.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: How would you like me to cave your head in for you?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: We’ve heard enough. Sit down. And don’t open your filthy mouth again.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: It’s very hard to keep personal prejudice out of a thing like this. And no matter where you run into it, prejudice obscures the truth. Nine of us now seem to feel that the defendant is innocent, but we’re just gambling on probabilities. We may be wrong. We may be trying to return a guilty man to the community. No one can really know. But we have a reasonable doubt, and this is a safeguard which has enormous value in our system. No jury can declare a man guilty unless it’s sure. We nine can’t understand how you three are still so sure. Maybe you can tell us.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I’ll try. But I still believe the boy is guilty for two reasons. One: the evidence given by the woman across the street who actually saw the murder committed.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: And how, brother! As far as I’m concerned that’s the most important testimony in the whole case.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: And two: the fact that this woman described the stabbing by saying she saw the boy raise his arm over his head and plunge the knife down into his father’s chest. She saw him do it – the wrong way.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: That’s right! That’s absolutely right!

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Now, let’s talk about this woman for a minute. She said that she went to bed at about eleven o’clock that night. Her bed was next to the window and she could look out while lying down and see directly into the boy’s window across the tracks. Finally, she turned towards the window about ten minutes after twelve, and, as she looked out, she saw the killing through the windows of the passing el train. She says that she got a good look at the boy in the act of stabbing his father. As far as I can see, this is unshakeable testimony.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: That’s what I mean. That’s the whole case.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: What do you think?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Well – I don’t know. There’s so much evidence to sift. This is a pretty complicated business.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: You can throw out all the other evidence. The woman saw him do it. What else do you want?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Well, maybe . . .

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Let’s vote on it.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Okay. There’s another vote called for. Anybody object?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: I’m changing my vote. I think he’s ‘guilty’.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Anybody else? The vote is eight to four.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: What makes you consider this one vote a personal triumph?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I’m the competitive type. Okay. Now here’s what I think. I think we’re a hung jury. Let’s take it inside to the judge.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: You didn’t want a hung jury before.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Well, I want it now.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I don’t understand that. You thought it was immoral to . . .

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I don’t any more. There are people in here who are so goddamned stubborn that you can’t even . . . We’ll never get this thing done. We’ll be here for a week. I say we’re a hung jury. Come on. You’re the leader of the cause. What about it?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Let’s go over it again.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: All right. Maybe we can talk about setting some kind of a time limit. The time is . . .

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Quarter after six.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Quarter after six. Someone before mentioned seven o’clock. I think that’s a point at which we might begin to discuss the question of whether we’re a hung jury or not.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Don’t you feel well?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I feel perfectly well – thank you. I was saying that seven o’clock would be a reasonable time to . . .

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: The reason I asked about that was because you were rubbing your nose like . . . I’m sorry for interrupting. But you made a gesture that reminded me . . .

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I’m trying to settle something here. Do you mind?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: I think this is important.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Very well.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Thank you. I’m sure you’ll pardon me for this, but I was wondering why you were rubbing your nose like that?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Ah, come on, now, will ya please!

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Right now I happen to be talking to this gentleman here. Now, why were you rubbing your nose?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Well, if it’s any of your business, I was rubbing it because it bothers me a little.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: I’m sorry. Is it because of your eyeglasses?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: It is. Now could we get on to something else?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Your eyeglasses make those deep impressions on the sides of your nose. I hadn’t noticed that before. They must be annoying.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: They are very annoying.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: The woman who testified that she saw the killing had these same deep marks on the sides of her nose.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: That’s right, she did. But I’ve been going over her face in my mind. She had those marks. She kept rubbing them in court.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: He’s right. She did do that a lot.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: This woman was about forty-five years old. She was making a tremendous effort to look thirty-five for her first public appearance. Heavy make-up. Dyed hair. No eyeglasses.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What d’ya mean, no glasses? You don’t know if she wore glasses. Just because she was rubbing her nose . . .

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: She had those marks. I saw ’em.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: So what? What d’ya think that means?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Listen, I saw ’em, too. He’s right. I was the closest one to her. She had these deep things, what d’ya call ’em, uh – you know.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Could those marks be made by anything other than eyeglasses?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: No. They couldn’t.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Listen, what are you saying here? I didn’t see any marks.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I did. Strange, but I didn’t think about it before.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Well, what about the lawyer? Why didn’t he say anything?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: There are twelve people in here concentrating on this case. Eleven of us didn’t think of it, either.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Okay. She had marks on her nose. I’m givin’ ya this. From glasses. Right? She never wore ’em out of the house so people’d think she was gorgeous. But when she saw this kid kill his father she was in the house. Alone. That’s all.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Do you wear your eyeglasses when you go to bed?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: No, I don’t. No one wears eyeglasses to bed.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: It’s logical to say that she wasn’t wearing them while she was in bed, tossing and turning, trying to fall asleep.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: How do you know?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I don’t know. I’m guessing. I’m also guessing that she probably didn’t have time to put glasses on then.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Wait a second . . .

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: And here’s another guess. Maybe she honestly thought she saw the boy kill his father. I say that she saw only a blur.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Maybe she was farsighted. Maybe they were sunglasses. What do you know about it?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I only know that the woman’s eyesight is in question now.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: She had to identify a person sixty feet away in the dark, without glasses.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: You can’t send someone off to die on evidence like that.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Don’t give me that!

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Don’t you think that the woman might have made a mistake?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: No!

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: It’s not possible?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: No! It’s not possible.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Is it possible?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Yes. I say not guilty.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Do you still think he’s guilty?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Yes, I think he’s guilty. But I couldn’t care less.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: How do you vote?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Not guilty. Do whatever you want.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: You’re the worst son a . . . I think he’s guilty.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Does anyone else think he’s guilty?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: No, I’m convinced.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What’s the matter with you?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I now have a reasonable doubt.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: It’s eleven to one.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Well, what about all the other evidence? What about all that stuff – the knife – the whole business?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: You said we could throw out all the other evidence.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: You’re alone.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I don’t care whether I’m alone or not. It’s my right.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: It’s your right.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Well, what d’ya want? I say he’s guilty.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: We want your arguments.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I gave you my arguments.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: We’re not convinced. We want to hear them again. We have as much time as it takes.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Everything – every single thing that came out in that courtroom, but I mean everything, says he’s guilty. Do you think I’m an idiot or something? You lousy bunch of bleeding hearts. You’re not goin’ to intimidate me. I’m entitled to my opinion. I can sit in this goddamn room for a year. Somebody say something. Why don’t’cha take that stuff about the old man – the old man who lived there – and heard everything. Or take the knife, what – just because – found one like it? The old man saw him. Right there on the stairs. What’s the difference how many seconds it took? What’s the difference? Every single thing. The knife falling through a hole in his pocket – you can’t prove that he didn’t get to the door. Sure you can hobble around the room all you want, but you can’t prove it. I’m telling you every single thing that went on has been twisted and turned in here. That business with the glasses, how do you know she didn’t have them on? The woman testified in court. Well, what d’ya want? That’s it. That’s the whole case. That whole thing about hearing the boy yell? The phrase was ‘I’m gonna kill you’. That’s what he said. To his own father. I don’t care what kind of a man that was. It was his father. That goddamn rotten kid. I know him. What they’re like. What they do to you. How they kill you every day. My God, don’t you see? How come I’m the only one who sees? Jeez, I can feel that knife goin’ in.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: It’s not your boy. He’s somebody else.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Let him live.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: All right. ‘Not guilty’.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: We’re ready.

script.speaker: Guard
script.text: All right, gentlemen. Put on your jackets and come along.
